q7.answer: The client never stores the key. On each outbound call it reads the current key from the in-memory snapshot (replaced whole by atomic reference swap on refresh) and puts it in the Authorization header, so the next request after a refresh uses the new key. An in-flight request keeps the key it started with.

q8.answer: A gate in step 7: query the cluster-internal version endpoint on each pod individually (not via the load balancer) and see V1 for all three secrets; kubectl shows every pod on the new image; each provider's usage view shows no old-key calls for at least one full refresh interval; and every other consumer from the step 1 inventory is moved or retired. Only then does security on-call disable the old keys.

q9.answer: Store access and KMS (step 2), then mint new keys and copy them into the store with old keys still active (step 3), then merge the code that reads from the store and removes the api_key lines from config/app.yaml with the CI guard (step 4, one PR), then roll out to prod with a canary pause (step 6), then confirm all instances use the new keys and revoke the old keys at the providers (step 7). Provider key creation happens before the switch and revocation after it. Keys are removed from the file in the same PR as the code switch, not as a separate later step.

q10.answer: By default make run sets APP_ENV=local, points base URLs at local stub servers that accept any key, and reads no secret. Optionally make run-sandbox sets APP_ENV=dev and the developer's own identity reads sandbox keys from orders-api/dev/*. Developers never get prod access, and a missing APP_ENV makes the app exit non-zero.

q11.answer: It treats the whole fetch as failed. It retries the whole fetch up to 3 more times, 2 seconds apart (4 attempts total). If any secret is still missing, it logs the error class and the secret names, exits non-zero, and never starts serving. /healthz is never 200 with only two keys.
